news.title: ‘He’s a smart guy’: Trump plans to discuss El-Sayed’s ‘Trumpcare’ proposals
news.text:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday described Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed as a "smart guy" and said he would meet him to discuss his proposal for universal healthcare. He also signalled an openness to finding common ground with congressional Democrats.
"He's a smart guy. He did a good job. He actually did a very good job. I know I'll be meeting with him. Maybe there's some place in the middle that we could go," Trump told The New York Post.
The remarks marked a remarkable shift for Trump, who repeatedly launched racist and Islamophobic attacks on El-Sayed during the midterm campaign. He described El-Sayed as a "jihadist" and said he would be the first senator to require a metal detector to enter Capitol Hill. Trump also urged voters to "send him back to where he came from" despite El-Sayed having been born in the United States.
The change in tone comes days after El-Sayed proposed that Democrats would name a universal cradle-to-grave healthcare programme 'Trumpcare' if the president agreed to support it. As part of the proposal, he shared an image of a gold-coloured card, a nod to Trump's well-known penchant for gold.
In an unexpected move, Trump shared illustrations of the proposed Trumpcare cards over the weekend on social media.
This is a message for @realDonaldTrump.
Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave. https://t.co/f32IYs3FXG
— Dr. Abdul El-Sayed (@AbdulElSayed) November 12, 2026
According to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), as many as four million Americans lost their health insurance after Trump's signature 'One Big Beautiful Bill' ended Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies. Costs also rose for many of those who remained insured.
Monthly premiums could have increased by as much as 114 per cent for up to 22 million Americans on ACA plans following the expiry of the subsidies, according to estimates by healthcare-focused organisation KFF.
Despite signalling openness to El-Sayed's proposal, Trump suggested that any agreement could be hard fought.
"I'm just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point I think they're going to want to negotiate. I will, and we can do health care. We can do a lot of great things together," Trump said.

news.title: Soybeans ease from four-week top, Brazilian planting weighs
news.text:
SINGAPORE: Chicago soybean futures slid on Wednesday for the first time in four sessions, with rapidly advancing Brazilian planting adding pressure on prices.

Wheat fell for a second session, while corn prices were largely unchanged.

“We had some gains in soybean prices over the last few days and the market is little bit lower today, given the planting progress we are seeing in Brazil,” said one trader in Singapore.

“We are likely to see pressure on prices unless there is a problem with the South American crop.” The most-active soybean contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) lost 0.7% to $12.25-1/2 a bushel, as of 0351 GMT.

Wheat fell 0.5% to $5.86-1/2 a bushel and corn was flat at $4.50-1/4 a bushel.

Brazilian farmers had planted 86% of the projected area of their 2026/27 soybean crop as of last Thursday, agribusiness consultancy AgRural said on Monday, up from 78% a week earlier and above 81% at the same time last year.

Rapidly advancing planting in Brazil, the world’s No. 1 exporter of the oilseed, is raising expectations of global supplies for early next year.

The soybean market was supported earlier this week by higher demand for US soymeal. Deforestation rules going into effect in the European Union in late December could steer soymeal export demand toward US supplies, analysts said, although a late postponement of EU rules is possible.

The US Department of Agriculture rated 54% of the US winter wheat crop as being in good-to-excellent condition in a weekly report on Monday, up from 53% last week.

Russian wheat export prices spiked last week following the trilateral summit of presidents Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China’s Shenzhen, analysts said.

 Nvidia’s Huang says he is in therapy as comeback rally fades 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP)—Jensen Huang apologised to Nvidia staff and said he was in therapy on Tuesday, as a stock rally triggered by his shock return as CEO faltered amid persistent doubts over the probes he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom.

“I made some terrible mistakes,” Huang told an hourlong all-hands meeting at the company’s Santa Clara, California, headquarters, The New York Times reported after reviewing a livestream of the event.

He told staff it was “not acceptable” that he had broken a code of conduct he had helped write, and dismissed suggestions that he was back because US President Donald Trump had pressured the board.

But Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been in contact with directors about Huang’s return. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump said. “And I convinced them.”

After vaulting more than 30 per cent on Monday, Nvidia shares were down about six per cent at close on Tuesday.

“The optimism faded quickly” for Nvidia, wrote Fawad Razaqzada of Forex.com, with “questions over corporate governance and board oversight still lingering.”

So far Monday’s surge was a “one day wonder…We are not seeing an upside follow through today at all,” said Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management.

– Trump pressure –

Huang resigned on November 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, a departure that sent shares in Nvidia and companies closely linked to the AI buildout tumbling.

Trump was reportedly talked into backing the return of the Taiwan-born CEO after top tech investors told him the US economy and Wall Street depended on it.

Nvidia said Monday that it had reinstated Huang as chief executive after receiving information from the US government that he did not pose a national security risk.

Trump is also an investor in Nvidia, owning as many as 370,000 shares in the company as of September 30, according to filings.

Shares linked to the AI boom have fallen steeply in recent weeks amid fears that the AI bubble, inflated since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, was finally bursting.

In downward-trending markets, quick rebounds are common but “tend to get negated and that has been the sequence since early October,” Mahoney said, adding that “sellers have absolute control of the market here.”

Nvidia is central to the AI investment story — its powerful processors are the key tool to train and run the AI models that are believed to be at the heart of a technological revolution.

The massive spending on its AI chips and software, housed in sprawling data centers, catapulted the company into the ranks of the world’s most valuable firms.

Huang used that success to turn Nvidia into a kind of central bank for other AI companies and startups, doling out loans and financial guarantees to firms that would otherwise struggle to borrow from traditional lenders.

– ‘Good corporate citizen’ –

Investors are also weighing a barrage of legal challenges facing Huang and Nvidia.

The board that let Huang go and then rehired him is still overseeing an internal investigation into concerns that he may have been the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, even though Trump says he has been cleared.

The Justice Department is separately investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that allegedly bought Nvidia processors and routed them to Chinese customers in violation of US export restrictions.

The Securities and Exchange Commission has also reportedly opened a probe into Nvidia’s accounting practices and potentially misleading communication to shareholders.

“Nvidia is a good corporate citizen. That shouldn’t be groundbreaking,” US Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters at an unrelated press conference in Washington on Tuesday.

“If Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn’t be the message that the president is saying to the American people,” he added.

Huang will nevertheless face lawmakers at a closed-door hearing before three House committees on December 1 and a livestreamed Senate committee hearing on December 3.

Lawmakers from both parties have expressed anger over the circumstances of Huang’s return, and the scrutiny is likely to intensify in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

news.title: US military base shooter seeks halt to firing squad execution
news.text:
Nidal Hasan, who is set to be executed by firing squad next month for his 2009 massacre at a US military base, asked a court on Tuesday to halt his execution, according to documents obtained by AFP.

The former US Army major and military psychiatrist asked a federal court to delay his execution, which is set for December 3, while he prepares a case to challenge it on constitutional grounds.

If the execution goes ahead, Hasan will be the first person killed by a US military firing squad since 1945.

A furore over plans to livestream the killing erupted in early October.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth initially said the execution would be “public” before a Pentagon spokesperson added it would be available online.

Concerns mounted far and wide about making the execution into a spectacle and turning Hasan into a martyr.

After days of debate and condemnation, US President Donald Trump cancelled the plans to broadcast the killing, while allowing some witnesses to observe it in person.

Hasan killed 13 people, including 12 soldiers, and wounded 30 others in his November 2009 rampage.

He was shot by a civilian police officer and is paralysed from the waist down.

During his trial, Hasan chose to conduct his own defence, and court-appointed attorneys raised concerns that he was seeking to be executed.

Ultimately, he was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013.
news.summary:
Nidal Hasan, set for a December 3 firing squad execution over the 2009 base massacre, has asked a US federal court to delay it on constitutional grounds.

news.title: Cyberattacks, outages and unanswered questions: Why America's digital infrastructure is having a a difficul...
news.text:
United States is currently struggling with its tech infrastructure. Last week, the nation faced Microsoft outage, which meant no Outlook, banking services were experiencing disruptions and flights across the country were grounded. While it may sound like a Hollywood apocalypse plot, this was really the case in the country. And the saga continues as the latest development involves three US intelligence agencies, including the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), which recently discovered a cybersecurity breach affecting some of their unclassified information.
According to a report by The New York Times, the compromised system was an open-source intelligence analysis network. It was designed to gather and analyse information available publicly, rather than handle classified material.
The National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence were also affected. Although the precise information accessed by the attackers remains unclear, officials have reportedly said that classified material was not compromised. The breach has since been contained.
US spy agencies hit by cyberattack
What makes the incident particularly concerning is the reported use of an artificial intelligence tool called Artex. Released in July by a Chinese engineer, the tool was originally developed to help organisations strengthen their cyber defences. However, security researchers and US officials have linked its subsequent misuse to numerous attacks on businesses across the world, including in Japan and South Korea.
Investigators have not established who was behind the intelligence agencies' breach. However, early indications have reportedly raised suspicions of possible Chinese involvement. Beijing's intelligence services and associated contractors have long been accused by Western officials of targeting US government networks and private businesses.
When technology failures become a national concern
The intelligence breach is only one part of a much larger picture. Over the past few weeks, several systems that underpin everyday life in America have experienced significant disruptions, leaving officials to explain what went wrong.
Microsoft was among the biggest names to face trouble. Its November 12-13 outage disrupted Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services. Governments, businesses and organisations across multiple countries, including the US, Japan and Australia, were affected.
The disruption lasted around 24 hours, making it one of the most significant service failures the company has experienced. It also exposed how dependent organisations have become on a relatively small number of technology providers.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella apologised publicly for the incident. The company has since launched what it calls a 'Code Red' initiative, placing engineering improvements and crisis response at the highest priority.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that internal company memos acknowledged the scale of the failure. Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, told employees that more customers had been left without email for longer than ever before.
"Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," Henderson said.
Microsoft has denied that the outage was caused by a cyberattack. Nevertheless, the disruption has added to questions about whether the company's existing infrastructure and engineering processes can cope with failures of this scale.
Other major organisations have also found themselves dealing with unexpected technical problems.
Apple experienced an internal systems failure that affected services such as iCloud and Apple Pay. The company said the disruption was triggered by an internal update and was not the result of a cyberattack.
United Airlines faced a technology failure that delayed approximately 150 flights. JPMorgan Chase also experienced a software problem that disrupted some banking services.
Meanwhile, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop that lasted around four-and-a-half hours. It was the longest halt to US air travel since the September 11 attacks in 2001.
Even America's intelligence networks are struggling
The disruptions have not spared government infrastructure either. The NSA recently experienced a day-long outage on its internal classified network, although the agency described the problem as a temporary degradation during routine maintenance.
It maintained that its mission-critical capabilities continued to operate.
US officials have insisted that the incidents are unrelated and that there is no evidence of a coordinated cyberattack behind the disruptions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, described the developments as unsettling but dismissed suggestions of malicious interference.
President Donald Trump has also played down the concerns. Speaking to reporters in Manila, he suggested that technical failures were inevitable when dealing with large and powerful organisations.
However, not everyone in Washington has been convinced. Republican Senator Josh Hawley questioned whether the incidents could simply be coincidences.
"If this is all a coincidence, it's like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world," he told reporters.
The FBI has also reportedly dealt with a breach involving its National Crime Information Center, a database used by law enforcement agencies across the country to exchange information about criminal suspects. Trump appeared to acknowledge the incident in an interview with Fox News, saying he did not like what had happened.
Separately, the US Agriculture Department discovered a cybersecurity incident that forced several internal applications to be taken offline.
Is AI making the problem harder to contain?
One possible explanation being discussed by cybersecurity experts is the growing role of AI in both finding vulnerabilities and exploiting them.
AI tools are increasingly capable of identifying weaknesses in software, automating attacks and helping hackers launch multiple intrusions at once. That makes defending large networks more complicated, particularly when organisations are dealing with legacy systems and interconnected services.
Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, recently offered an explanation for the NSA disruption. He attributed it to software patches deployed to address a PHP vulnerability identified using AI. The flaw could potentially allow attackers to take remote control of servers.
Speaking to Fox Business, Clayton suggested that the process of fixing vulnerabilities was itself creating technical challenges. As organisations upgrade their systems, he said, some are failing to restart as expected or are struggling to communicate properly with other connected systems.
The Washington Sun also reported, citing three people familiar with private discussions, that the NSA and Wall Street executives had told lawmakers that AI had helped identify vulnerabilities requiring fixes. The subsequent patches reportedly placed temporary pressure on systems.
For Cynthia Kaiser, a former senior FBI cyber official and current senior vice-president at Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center, the incidents point to a broader problem.
She warned that disruptions across different industries demonstrate how closely connected digital infrastructure has become, allowing a single technical failure or software update to trigger consequences far beyond the system where it originated.
And that may be the biggest concern facing the US right now. The country is not dealing with one clearly identified cyberattack or a single malfunctioning network. It is dealing with several disruptions across government agencies, airlines, banks and technology companies, each raising questions about preparedness and resilience.
Officials may be right that these incidents are unrelated. But when email services, intelligence networks, banking systems and air travel all experience disruption within weeks, simply calling them coincidences does little to reassure the public. The bigger question is whether the infrastructure supporting modern America is keeping pace with the technology, threats and demands placed upon it.

news.title: Revealed: When UK households will receive £100 energy payment from the government
news.text:
More than 20 million households across the UK will begin receiving a £100 cash payment from January 4 to help with the rising cost of energy bills, ministers have announced. 

The measure, unveiled at the autumn Budget, gives an automatic £100 rebate to properties in council tax bands A to D. 

But with a typical household set to pay £62 a week for energy from January, the money will only cover the first 11 days of the new year, researchers have warned. 

Councils will begin making payments from 4 January, the Treasury said as it set out more details of how the rebate will work. 

A total of 13 million households who pay by direct debit will automatically receive the payment directly into their bank accounts, with no action required. 

Those who pay in other ways will be contacted and given the choice of receiving the £100 into their bank account or as credit against their council tax bill. 

In a bid to ensure no-one loses out, the scheme will remain open until the end of May.

Chancellor John Healey said: “Families are worried about energy bills rising again this winter.” 

In what appeared to be a reference to Donald Trump’s war in Iran, he added: “Whilst we can’t control movements in global energy markets, we’re doing what we can to protect household finances and give families some breathing space.

“That’s why 20 million households will receive £100 from January. Today we’re setting out how money will be paid to families straight into their bank accounts.”

Ofgem’s energy price cap is set to rise by £443 in the new year, forecaster Cornwall Insight has predicted, taking the average bill from £1,723 to £2,166 – a 26 per cent increase. 

This would mark the highest level since 2023. 

The bleak outlook for bills comes after escalating violence in the Middle East sparked a fresh jump in oil and gas prices last month.

Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: “Too many families up and down the country are worried about the costs of putting on the heating this winter.

“That’s why we’re giving millions of people breathing space with their energy bills, and supporting councils to act quickly to ensure everyone eligible gets the support they are entitled to.

“We will continue to do everything we can to support people and bring bills down for good, by breaking the link with fossil fuels and delivering more clean, homegrown power.”
news.summary: More than 20 million household in council tax bands A-D to get the payment into their bank accounts next year

news.title: Trump awards highest honour Medal of Freedom to ex-New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani
news.text:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday awarded the Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honour, to disgraced former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani.
Trump had promised to honour Giuliani last year and described him as the "greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot".
While the ceremony was not televised, the White House shared a photograph on X and said: "America's Mayor receives America's highest civilian honor. President Donald J Trump awards Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom for true American leadership and a lifetime of public service."
Once celebrated as 'America's Mayor' for his leadership in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, Giuliani later became the public face of Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election. He has been among Trump's closest allies since he first ran for office in 2016.
America's Mayor receives America's highest civilian honor. 🇺🇸
President Donald J. Trump awards @RudyGiuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom for true American leadership and a lifetime of public service. https://t.co/dS1wd4irkI
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 24, 2026
For his role in challenging the 2020 election results, Giuliani was disbarred in New York and Washington DC, and agreed to pay $148 million to two Georgia election workers over false claims about their role in the election.
Giuliani was also named a co-conspirator alongside Trump in the federal election interference case related to the 2020 election. He was separately indicted in Arizona, along with several others, over efforts to overturn the state's election result. Both cases have since been dropped.
From national hero to disgraced loyalist
Giuliani has had one of the most remarkable trajectories in modern American public life.
In the 1980s, Giuliani rose to prominence for taking on organised crime. In the 2000s, he became known as 'America's Mayor' by becoming the symbol of leadership and resilience in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks.
Today, however, Giuliani is best known for his loyalty to Trump and the lengths to which he went in support of efforts to overturn the 2020 election result.
Giuliani was one of Trump's closest advisers during the 2016 presidential campaign and later served as his personal lawyer during Trump's first term in office.
After Trump lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, Giuliani joined efforts to overturn the outcome and repeatedly promoted false claims that Trump had won.
Federal prosecutors later indicted Giuliani alongside Trump over attempts to overturn the 2020 election. He was also found liable for defaming two Georgia election workers and agreed to pay them $148 million. He was separately indicted in Arizona in another election-related case that was later dropped.

news.title: Uddhav Sena takes a dig at PM Modi over market crash, asks 'Where is PM's influence?'
news.text: Digital Desk | Mumbai, Nov 25 (IANS) The Shiv Sena (UBT) on Wednesday launched a sharp attack on Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the central government after a steep stock market sell-off on Monday coincided with the release of the Lowy Institute’s Asia Power Index 2026, which ranked India third among Asia’s most powerful nations and placed Modi as the region’s second-most effective leader behind Chinese President Xi Jinping. The Sena Thackeray camp, in the party mouthpiece ‘Saamana’ editorial, questioned the contrast between international power rankings and heavy losses suffered by retail investors, asking "Where has Modi’s 'influence' gone?" and "Whose progress is this really?" Pointing to the Australia-based Lowy Institute report, the editorial asked whether the think tank’s index is real or the falling Sensex, arguing that India's purported status as a major regional power failed to prevent the market's steepest single-day drop in four months. "When Modi is being rated the second-most effective leader and India is being called a 'major power' in Asia, it is not a good sign if Indian investors lose lakhs of crores," commented the editorial. The editorial alleged that ordinary investors are losing lakhs of crores every few months, citing a "Black Wednesday" in September that wiped out around Rs 4 lakh crore and Monday’s "Black Monday" rout erasing roughly Rs 5 lakh crore in investor wealth. Questioning the government’s emphasis on high GDP growth and economic dynamism, the editorial noted that market falls continue despite official growth narratives and global commentary, including remarks by U S President Donald Trump praising India’s economy. Uddhav Thackeray-led Shiv Sena noted that while September’s slide followed selling pressure in the U S government bond market, Monday’s drop was driven by profit booking, alongside recurring factors such as fears of U S Federal Reserve rate hikes, rupee weakness, inflation pressures on foreign investors, and heavy losses in banking stocks. "The Modi government may boast loudly about economic progress, but if a 'Black Day' is going to dawn in the stock market every four months and wipe out lakhs of crores, whose progress is this really?" it asked. The editorial claimed that while the wealth of select industrialists close to the administration grows in billions, small investors bear the brunt of periodic market crashes.

news.title: Let’s hope Trump is willing to take his winnings and go quietly
news.text:
One of the reasons Republicans lost the midterm elections so badly is that a significant portion of their voters realised that they had been conned. People who had voted for Donald Trump’s party for the past decade stayed at home or even voted Democratic. Trump, they saw, was a charlatan who had broken his promises to keep the United States out of foreign wars, to bring down inflation and to “drain the swamp” of Washington of corruption. 

But what will the con man do now that he has been found out? That is the biggest question in US politics today. While Trump has been remarkably quiet since the midterms, his personality and actions offer clues that point toward two competing scenarios.

The most hopeful possibility is that Trump, as he has often done, takes his winnings and cuts his losses. The true con man, after all, doesn’t care what happens to his marks after he’s taken their money. And Trump has used his second term in office to enrich himself and his family to a staggering degree. Falsely claiming he was a billionaire helped Trump win the presidency, but it is only holding the office that enabled him to become an actual billionaire. 

Trump will be able to get away with all this. Recent US supreme court rulings give presidents a high degree of impunity and Trump can offer unconditional pardons to his inner circle and maybe even to himself. To assuage his ego, Trump can leave monuments to his power in the physical landscape of Washington, most notably in his renovation of the White House’s East Wing, a project to which he has devoted much of his attention.

There are signs that Trump is dissociating himself from the Republican Party. After the midterms results became clear, he blamed other Republicans. Trump claimed that if he himself had been on the ballot, they would have won in a landslide. As delusional as this view is, it is one that was not available to Trump when he lost the 2020 election. Psychologically, Trump cannot allow himself to be seen as a loser. But now, instead of having to discredit election results and foment a violent insurrection, Trump can merely claim that it’s other Republicans who are the losers. In his own mind, he can remain a winner, having been “victorious” in three presidential elections in a row.

[ The scale of corruption in Trump’s second administration is head-spinningOpens in new window ]

Trump is not Nigel Farage or Marine Le Pen. He did not spend his life building a political movement. While he has always held certain basic political instincts, he came late to politics. Until he ran for president, he wasn’t even a Republican. 

It is a sorry commentary on the state of US politics that the best-case scenario is that Trump uses the presidency to enrich himself and escapes without any consequences. But the alternative – that Trump doubles down on his Make America Great Again (Maga) agenda – is far more dangerous.

Trump may be a con man, but he craves attention and adulation. His father, Fred Trump, was content to defraud the US federal government by overestimating building costs for public housing projects. (Fred was frequently investigated, though never indicted.) 

Making money alone was never enough for Donald, however. He also wanted to be a celebrity. Few real estate developers became as famous as he did in the 1980s. Often pretending to be a publicist named John Barron, Trump frequently called the tabloid press to report on his doings. Most infamously, he reported to the New York Post that his girlfriend Marla Maples had claimed that Trump gave her “the best sex I ever had”. Is a man who craves the spotlight so much going to be content with just escaping with the loot? 

Trump probably cannot regain the support of the voters he lost. Even if he puts an end to the Iran war and brings down inflation, voters who realise they have been tricked by Trump are unlikely to come back to him. The only place Trump can receive adoration is among his hard-core Maga base. But that suggests that instead of moderating his policies in response to his midterm defeat, Trump may radicalise them.

The clearest sign that Trump might be doubling down on Maga is his appointment of Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff. This is a key position in any presidential administration as the chief of staff manages day-to-day operations, controls access to the president, and is their top adviser. Miller is the most right-wing person in Trump’s circle, the architect in Trump’s first term of his cruel family separation policy for migrants at the border and of Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s invasion of US cities in his second term. The Southern Poverty Law Centre characterises Miller as an advocate of “open white nationalism” based on leaked emails in which he, for example, promoted the racist great replacement theory.

[ ‘He’s a great fighter’: Stephen Miller, the man shaping Trump’s final actOpens in new window ]

In Miller, Trump has also chosen someone with a famously pugnacious personality. This suggests that, instead of disengaging, Trump is gearing up for a fight. Miller acknowledges few checks on presidential authority. With him in charge, Trump may push his constitutional authority well beyond its limits to bypass a Democratic Congress. 

Miller believes that true Americans – those of European descent – are losing out to hordes of non-white migrants. That Maga has only two more years in power will make Miller even more desperate to enact his far-right vision for the US. And he can only do so by undermining American democracy.

How far Trump goes along with Miller will determine the rest of his second term. If Trump decides Miller isn’t serving his interests, he won’t hesitate to discard him. For Trump, loyalty is a one-way street.

[ Maureen Dowd: Donald Trump breaks the law so fast that the law is left in his orange dustOpens in new window ]

Trump’s personality has dominated US politics for more than a decade, but as he enters his final two years in office as an unpopular lame duck, he will be torn in two directions. He can simply leave the presidency as a very rich man who never has to pay for his crimes. Or he can fight to remain a hero to the Maga faithful by pushing a radicalised agenda. Let’s hope that Trump, like many US voters, realises that he is a con man and is content with getting away with it.
news.summary: The best-case scenario is that the US president enriches himself and avoids consequences. The alternative could be far worse
news.author: Daniel Geary

news.title: Watergate Legend Bob Woodward Reveals His One Source He Wanted To Name
news.text: After more than half a century as one of the world's most famous journalists, Bob Woodward still isn't quite used to being on the receiving end of an interview."If you ask something, I may naturally ask you a question," says the 83-year-old author and longtime Washington Post reporter, adding that being a celebrity is "the reality, it is the TV media era, and you just deal with it."The average journalist doesn't live like Woodward, who spoke recently from the living room of the longtime residence he shares with his wife and fellow reporter, Elsa Walsh: a 19th-century Georgetown townhouse with enough grandeur to merit a profile in Architectural Digest. But he still identifies as a working journalist, ever curious about the story behind the headlines.Woodward made his name in the 1970s as one of the defining outsiders, a recent hire at the Post who helped break the Watergate scandal and bring down President Richard Nixon. In the decades following, Woodward became a veritable brand for inside stories on Washington power, with a long run of bestselling books on the White House, the Supreme Court, the intelligence community and the military leadership. Denied access to Nixon, he has since met with sitting presidents from both major political parties, from Democrat Jimmy Carter to Republican Donald Trump, and has become as much a Washington fixture as the leaders of a given administration."I may be able to talk to presidents," he says. "Sometimes they say interesting things, but the real interesting information comes from people who are close to the president, who work for the president."In his new book, "Secrets: A Reporter's Memoir," out Tuesday, Woodward tells his own story, sharing his worldview and how it connects with his job. Woodward defines himself as a longtime skeptic whose first real work of investigation was into his parents' marriage, which appeared to him so troubled that, at age 11, he searched their bedroom and found a letter from his mother to his father referring to "our divorce." Woodward confronted his father, who confirmed the breakup."You have to snoop," Woodward writes in his memoir. "You must look everywhere things could be hidden because they are hidden."Woodward opens up about himself in "Secrets" and, to some controversy, about some of his sources - from former national security adviser Brent Scowcroft to former White House aide Richard Darman, with whom Woodward formed a close friendship. In a note to readers, Woodward writes that many of the sources had died or acknowledged their ties to him in their own books, papers and oral histories. Some living sources declined permission to be named "because they are afraid of reprisal from the current government," he writes.During his interview with The Associated Press, Woodward discussed his reluctance to identify with political ideologies, his disappointment in Washington Post owner Jeff Bezos and the unflagging rush of door-knocking, a practice he vows to maintain even if he must knock with a cane. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.WOODWARD: Yes, if possible. I mean the object in a book like this is to take people as close as possible, and who the sources are and what they're saying and their demeanor is very important.WOODWARD: There's one source who had given me some top-secret information and I went to him and I said, "I'd like to name you and tell the story of our relationship," and he said, "Absolutely not." But everyone else, I think, kind of accepts this is history. And the goal here is history.WOODWARD: I did (tell) some people - this story is coming out. And interestingly enough, I heard no objections from any family member or anyone who was close. People are always interested in history. And even if it's history about somebody they know. But it was a very careful process. And there was so much on the public record. There are actually files in universities where people have put away their papers that include discussions of interviews with me.WOODWARD: Well, that was the promise, and I thought it was more likely he could deliver on it.WOODWARD: I don't think in those terms. I do vote, but it's based on the tradition of the presidency, of somebody using the office for - I'm a little idealistic here - for high purpose. And sometimes they do. Too often they don't.WOODWARD: I indeed did not.WOODWARD: He has not.WOODWARD: I have not. And I said critical things about him. I thought the owner of The Washington Post should not go to the presidential inauguration of Donald Trump. Katharine Graham, the owner of the Post, during the 1970s, never would have done that. I don't think the owner of a newspaper should get close to politicians.WOODWARD: He was a drug addict, and that's what killed John Belushi, the comedian. And it's a very sad story. I couldn't launder it. I couldn't say he was, you know, kidnapped or something like that, as I think some of his supporters wish had been the case. I spent a good deal of time communicating what a great humorist Belushi was. What a great actor he was. And, people don't remember that.WOODWARD: I mean, that's absurd. That's a joke. ... I understand the family and people close to Belushi would like to say, you know, this can't be true. But it was true.WOODWARD: You've got to. I learned that from my former colleague Carl Bernstein, when we were reporting on Watergate. He had much more experience than I, and he said we will get nowhere talking to people in their offices. And if we make an appointment, they'll bring in some handler to observe. We are going to have to make the reporter's equivalent of the cold call, but the cold call isn't by phone. It's showing up at the door of people who have knowledge.Not long ago there was a general I wanted to talk to - emails, phone messages, nothing. I found out where he lived, and I went there. You can't go too late. You can't go too early. About 8:15 p.m. was the perfect time. And I knocked on his door, and he opened the door and he recognized me and he said, "Are you still doing this (expletive)?" But he invited me in.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Bob Woodward made his name in the 1970s as one of the defining outsiders, a recent hire at the Post who helped break the Watergate scandal and bring down President Richard Nixon.

news.title: Nvidia board faces scrutiny after reversing Jensen Huang’s resignation
news.text:
Nvidia board joins Jensen Huang under scrutiny after reinstating embattled CEO

New York: Jensen Huang has been under a spotlight for weeks, but after the 11-day period of disorder that included the resignation and reinstatement of the Nvidia executive, the company’s board is joining him at the centre of scrutiny.

The 10-person board voted unanimously to rehire Huang as Nvidia’s president, CEO and a fellow board member, writing in an announcement Monday that the decision emerged after discussions with Huang and input from senior levels of the United States government. President Donald Trump said he believes his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement.

Just six days earlier, the board was singing a different tune. Board members had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation following his admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The board did not intend to reinstate him, Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of a quarterly earnings call.

To bow to pressure to bring someone back who has hurt the reputation of the company is crazy, said Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School.

The board’s stunning reversal has spurred questions about its independence and what Trump’s role means for the meeting of business and politics.

Concerns swirl about corporate governance and Trump’s intervention

Nvidia’s board includes both business leaders with longstanding ties to the company and a group of more recent additions who have experience at big-name companies including Taco Bell, PepsiCo and Eli Lilly.

Some experts have called for the board to resign in the wake of the havoc.

Day, who has expertise in financial crises and corporate governance, emphasised that the board has a duty to represent shareholders, not the CEO.

The shareholders should demand a new board, she said.

Corporate governance experts say long tenures for board members can compromise their independence. Under the rules of the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, companies are required to have a majority of directors who are independent.

Traditionally, it’s a good practice to limit how long people can sit on a board, said Nada Kakabadse, professor of policy, governance and ethics at the University of Reading’s Henley Business School. They should be eight years maximum. Four years, plus another four years if they’re performing well. But beyond that, they really become not independent anymore, right

It’s not unusual for US tech bosses to stuff their boards with allies or high-profile figures who might not be aware of what’s happening at the company, Kakabadse said.

American business has a culture of leader heroes — entrepreneurs who founded companies and are seen as the only ones who can steer them through tough times, she said. But at some point, the companies can get so big that you need proper corporate structure, you need proper governance.

Many people are also questioning what input the company received from senior government leaders and why it persuaded the board to make a complete turnaround.

The board should have listened to the president’s request and stuck to its position that it was time to find a new CEO, said Peter Cohan, an associate professor of management practice at Babson College. In my opinion, by giving in to Trump, the board is endangering the company. That’s because Huang has seen that he can do anything he wants, and he will get away with it.

The idea of an independent board of experts looking out for the long-term interests of the company and its shareholders sort of goes out the window if the sitting president essentially tells them what to do, said Daniel Kinderman, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Delaware.

This is really the mark of crony capitalism, right he said.

Kinderman said the episode might open the door a little bit more for more aggressive actions on behalf of elected representatives in their relationships with businesses.

Lawmakers call for accountability from the board

The Nvidia saga has made waves in Washington, particularly in conversations around export controls. Huang’s affair raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with those restrictions. The reinstatement has renewed fervour on Capitol Hill for more transparency from both Huang and the board.

Elected officials from both parties were quick to respond to the reinstatement with criticism and scepticism.

Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, said the decision to bring Huang back was reckless. She wrote in a statement Monday that it does not change the fact that Huang, Nvidia executives and the company’s board still owe Congress answers.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, called for both Huang and the board to testify publicly to Congress. A boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk, she said in a statement Monday.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is investigating Nvidia in connection with Huang’s affair, said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that the president’s intervention does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favour.

The California Department of Justice said Thursday that it is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public.

Some members joined the Nvidia board in the 1990s

Two board members, Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, joined the board in 1993 when Nvidia was founded. Stevens and Coxe were both previously venture capitalists who made early investments in Nvidia.

Two other long-serving board members, Jones and Brooke Seawell, are the former chief executive and chief financial officer, respectively, of Synopsys, which makes chip-design software and counted Nvidia as its first customer. Jones joined Nvidia’s board in 1993, while Seawell joined four years later.

Stephen Neal, who’s designated as the board’s lead independent director, joined in 2019. He’s the chairman emeritus of Cooley LLP, Nvidia’s longtime law firm, and has advised the company in various governance matters, according to his bio.

Other board members have less of a direct link to Nvidia.

Melissa Lora, former president of Taco Bell International, spent 31 years at the fast food company and joined Nvidia’s board in 2023. Aarti Shah, formerly a senior vice president and chief digital officer at pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly, joined in 2020.

John Dabiri, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology whose lab researches fluid mechanics, was added to the board in 2020. Dawn Hudson was the NFL’s chief marketing officer and a former CEO of Pepsi-Cola’s North American division who has been on the board since 2013. Suzanne Nora Johnson was a vice chair at Goldman Sachs and joined the board in July.

None of the board members provided comment in response to requests from The Associated Press.

The 10-person board voted unanimously […]

news.title: John McManus: Look out Ireland, nothing says AI bubble quite like the return of Jensen Huang
news.text:
Jensen Huang is many things: technology visionary, natty dresser and a man in trouble with his wife. He is also the glue that holds together the stuttering artificial intelligence (AI) boom. 

His reinstatement as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday – following his resignation over an extramarital affair with a businesswoman alleged to be linked to Chinese intelligence – sent the company’s shares up 30 per cent and led a rally for technology stocks. It may well prove short lived. 

The return of Huang had the ringing endorsement of the US president. “The country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy,” according to Donald Trump. US treasury secretary Scott Bessent was equally enthused, singing along with a chorus of AI “leaders” led by Elon Musk. 

In many ways that should be all the warning we need. Nothing says bubble quite like the idea that one man can add more than a trillion dollars to the price of a company’s shares and drive-up global stock markets simply by being unfired. The fetishisation of “founders” is routine in Silicon Valley, but irrational exuberance does not even come close to describing the response to Huang’s return. 

Huang and Nvidia are central to the boom in tech stocks that now account for almost 40 per cent of the US market by value. They not only make the chips at the heart of the technology, they have driven the market for their products with $700 billion (€638 billion) of financing to their customers.

[ How Donald Trump was lobbied to bring back Nvidia’s Jensen HuangOpens in new window ]

Nvidia’s business model – and those of its peers – relies on some pretty heroic assumptions about the uptake of AI and the price that users will pay for it. The massive but strangely lacklustre listing of Anthropic last week presaged a global sell off in tech stocks that demonstrated that the credibility of the assumptions underlying the boom are finally being tested. Questions are being asked about everything from the return on capital to consumer demand. Greater oversight is on the way once the Democrats take control of the US Congress in the new year. 

The seed of doubt has been planted and the return of the industry’s chief “hype man” Huang is unlikely to reassure the market. We should desperately hope that it does, because if there is one country that really does not want the bubble to burst, it is Ireland. 

Despite waning public support, we have quietly gone all-in on building data centres to feed the supposedly insatiable demand of AI for “compute” – the latest verb to become a noun and turned into an asset class by big tech.

According to Dublin-based consultants Bit Power, there is the best part of €22 billion committed to building new data centres here, which will double the size of Irish “compute”. It is arguably the biggest pipeline of any European country, although such things are difficult to measure. As a percentage of the economy – as measured by gross domestic product – it is right up there. And so are the consequences if the bubble bursts. 

The full economic benefit – and the potential hit – of this investment could be double when you take into account the other activity generated.

[ Jensen Huang has the affair – his wife gets the performance review. Some things never changeOpens in new window ]

Despite the well-ventilated concerns about the prices and availability of electricity, we remain competitive, even when up against locations in Scandinavia that have cheaper power. 

We have a couple of things in our favour, including better connectivity via transatlantic cables landing in Ireland. But our real strength is the cluster of technology companies here that includes some so-called hyperscalers – Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta Platforms and others – who are going hell for leather to try to dominate the market for AI.

They already own two thirds of the capacity of the existing 109 data centres, according to Bit Power. They will directly own about 13 per cent of the capacity of the 59 data centres in the pipeline. The rest of the new “compute” will be owned by third parties who will lease capacity to the hyperscalers and other users. 

These third-party data-centre backers are like property developers who went all-in on office blocks before the 2008 crash. If things don’t work out they will be left with a lot of expensive servers sitting idle. The people who lent them money will have a problem. If they are relying on vendor financing from equipment manufacturers – like that provided by Nvidia to its customers – the contagion will be quick and extreme. 

[ John FitzGerald: I’ve done some sums and concluded many AI investors could lose their shirtsOpens in new window ]

But that is only part of the problem. The other is what happens to the wider Irish businesses of the hyperscalers, which employ thousands of people, if things don’t work out according to plan. It will be a double whammy to end all double whammies.
news.summary: A €22bn pipeline of data centres leaves the Irish economy exposed. Markets cheering the Nvidia chief’s comeback should make us nervous
news.author: John McManus

news.title: Trump thanks Mirziyoyev for Uzbek pavilions gifted to US
news.text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 25. US President
Donald Trump has thanked Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev for
gifting traditional Uzbek wooden pavilions to the United States
ahead of the country's 250th anniversary of independence.

Trump shared his remarks on his Truth Social account, praising
the craftsmanship of the Uzbek artisans who built the
structures.

He said it had been a special honor to fly over the pavilions
aboard Marine One during a presentation ceremony last week attended
by Uzbekistan's Ambassador to the United States Furqat Sidikov and
US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

Trump highlighted that the pavilions were made from 200-year-old
walnut wood and praised the Uzbek craftsmen for their dedication,
noting that they had spent several months away from their families
working on the project, including in challenging weather
conditions.

The US president said he had decided to make the pavilions
available for public use rather than keep them as personal
property. They have been installed along the Tidal Basin in
Washington, D.C., in an area offering views of the Jefferson
Memorial and the Washington Monument.

Trump also expressed hope that the pavilions would become one of
the city's popular attractions following the opening of the
National Heroes Garden next year. He said the site could host
diplomatic receptions, cultural events, photo opportunities during
the National Cherry Blossom Festival and other public
gatherings.

"Uzbekistan's skilled craftsmen are true artists! They built
these beautiful pavilions with exceptional craftsmanship. They are
truly magnificent!" Trump wrote.

He also thanked the Embassy of Uzbekistan in Washington and the
U.S. National Park Service for their cooperation in carrying out
the project.

The pavilions were presented as a gift showcasing Uzbekistan's
traditional architectural heritage and the craftsmanship of its
artisans to the American public.

news.title: Who is Alexa D’Agostino? GTA 6 writer accused of 'teaching women to manipulate' men as old dating advice blog posts resurface online
news.text: Alexa D’Agostino, a Rockstar Games writer who worked on Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), has become the centre of an online controversy after her old blog posts and social media activity resurfaced following the game's release. The writer, who contributed to the development of Lucia Caminos, one of GTA 6's two protagonists, is facing criticism over decade-old dating advice, personal essays and political posts.The controversy has intensified after her X account, reportedly operating under @lexidisco, disappeared. As gamers question her past remarks and their alleged connection to Lucia's characterisation, here is everything to know about Alexa D’Agostino, her Rockstar Games career and the backlash.Alexa D’Agostino is a writer at Rockstar Games who has worked on several projects associated with the studio. Her credits include Grand Theft Auto VI, Grand Theft Auto Online, Red Dead Redemption 2, Red Dead Online and Grand Theft Auto V. She has also worked in development and production on interactive entertainment projects for Nickelodeon.According to her professional profile, her earlier work included projects such as Nickelodeon Basketball Stars 2, Nickelodeon Soccer Stars 2 and Nickelodeon Tag Attack. However, GTA 6 has brought her work to a much larger gaming audience, particularly because of her involvement in developing Lucia Caminos, one of the game's two protagonists. D’Agostino discussed her approach to Lucia in an October 2026 interview with LOVE magazine. She explained that the character was partly inspired by women she knew personally, including her mother, an immigrant who grew up in Newark, New Jersey.D’Agostino's comments in the LOVE interview have become particularly relevant following the backlash. She described her mother as someone who was "rowdy, kind, but not to take any shit", explaining that she recognised several of those qualities in Lucia. She also spoke about wanting to create a character who felt like a complete person rather than someone designed around a particular stereotype. D’Agostino said that giving a character her own desires and imperfections could make her feel authentic.She described the result as "perfectly imperfect" and said she wanted Lucia to be a woman who could "stand tall next to the likes of Arthur Morgan and Niko Bellic". However, she is not the sole writer responsible for GTA 6's narrative. Rockstar's narrative leadership includes Rupert Humphries, its senior vice president of narrative, alongside several other writers and developers. GTA 6 ATM robbery guide: How to steal an ATM with a tow truck and get the moneyThe controversy gained attention around November 22, when social media users began circulating material allegedly connected to D’Agostino's old personal blog, theyearofalexa.com. The website, which was active around 2015 to 2018 and has been preserved through the Wayback Machine, reportedly contained personal essays, creative writing, poems and lifestyle advice.One particular post about meeting a new boyfriend's friends became a major talking point. It offered suggestions about handling different social situations, observing group dynamics, avoiding excessive drinking and making a good first impression. However, critics took issue with the language used in the article, particularly references to finding a "new man" and a boyfriend as a "boytoy". Some interpreted the advice as encouraging women to manipulate or use men rather than build genuine relationships.One X user claimed that the writer had a blog "where she writes blogs teaching girls how to manipulate and take advantage of men". The criticism spread across multiple accounts, with screenshots and archived material being shared as evidence. However, the blog also contained ordinary dating and social advice, and describing its entire contents as a manual for manipulating men would be an exaggerated interpretation.GTA 6 weather system guide: Why it is not raining, when storms appear, and how to fix itThe blog was not the only material being discussed. Older posts and retweets allegedly associated with D’Agostino's former X account, @lexidisco, also began circulating. One particularly discussed post reportedly involved a remark about having a bad day and imagining how much harder things would be if she also had children. Netizens interpreted it as dismissive of parenthood, while others viewed it as an old personal remark being taken out of context.Her political activity also attracted attention. Screenshots circulated of posts critical of Donald Trump, including allegations concerning Epstein and Mar-a-Lago, alongside other progressive-leaning content. These posts became part of a wider argument about the political and cultural direction of GTA 6. Some players attempted to connect her personal views to Lucia's personality and the game's relationship dynamics. One account discussing the controversy wrote: "The writer of Lucia, the character that makes Jason do everything, wrote a blog about manipulating men?" Another recurring criticism was that Rockstar had moved away from the storytelling style associated with earlier GTA protagonists.Lucia's characterisation has already attracted considerable discussion among players, particularly regarding her relationship with Jason Duval. Some critics believe the game's relationship dynamics give Lucia too much control, while Jason is sometimes portrayed as reactive or less assertive. Others have defended the characters, arguing that their contrasting personalities are central to the story.D’Agostino's old blog posts have now become another talking point in these discussions. Critics have suggested that her personal attitudes could have influenced the way Lucia was written. However, there is no verified evidence establishing that the dating advice on her old website directly influenced Lucia's dialogue, decisions or relationship with Jason. news.title: Trump says he'll meet with El-Sayed on Medicare for All proposal
news.text:
President Donald Trump said he plans to meet with Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss Medicare for All, a long-standing progressive health care proposal that the incoming Democrat supported during his campaign.

In an interview with the New York Post on Nov. 24, Trump praised El-Sayed's effort to brand the single-payer health care plan under a "Trumpcare" label, calling the freshman Democrat "a smart guy" and suggesting there could be room for compromise.

"He did a good job. He actually did a very good job," Trump said of El-Sayed’s pitch, according to the Post. "I know I’ll be meeting with him. Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go."

El-Sayed, a doctor and former public health official who was elected to the Senate from Michigan this month, campaigned in support of Medicare for All, a proposal that would provide government-backed health coverage to all Americans. Medicare currently covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities.

The Democratic senator-elect has spent recent weeks urging Trump to consider Medicare for All. Earlier this month, he posted an image on social media of a gold card labeled "TrumpCare" and called on the president to guarantee health care coverage "from cradle to grave." Trump later surprised political observers by sharing a screenshot of El-Sayed's post on his own Truth Social platform.

'On the table': Can Trump and progressive Dems reach a deal on Medicare for All?

"Let's get to work, then. Ready when you are," El-Sayed wrote on social media after Trump shared the post.

Appearing on NBC’s "Meet the Press" on Nov. 22, El-Sayed said Trump had "signaled openness" to discussing Medicare for All. He argued that if Trump wanted to cement his place in history, he could champion a program that guarantees coverage for every American.

"There is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card," El-Sayed said, describing a health care card Americans could carry "from the moment they are born to the moment that they pass away."

news.title: Trump to meet Democrat El-Sayed on 'Trumpcare' health plan: 'We can do a lot together' - report
news.text:
US President Donald Trump will meet with Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss passing the Michigan Democrat's "Medicare for All" plan under the name "Trumpcare," he told the New York Post in an Oval Office interview on Tuesday.

"He's a smart guy," Trump said of El-Sayed. "He did a good job. He actually did a very good job."

The president gave no date for the talks. "I know I'll be meeting with him," he added. "Maybe there's some place in the middle that we could go."

El-Sayed has pitched a golden insurance card that would give every American health coverage and carry the "Trumpcare" name. He posted a mockup on social media and tagged the president.

"Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee health care for every American, from cradle to grave," he wrote. El-Sayed later told NPR he does not care about the label. "Put his name on it," he remarked. "He'll probably pass it. I'm not above doing that."

The friendly words are a sharp turn from the midterm campaign. Back then, Trump described El-Sayed as a "jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you," and El-Sayed accused him of "hateful" rhetoric.

Democrats will control the House and Senate in January, and Trump expects them to come to the table. "I'm just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point I think they're going to want to negotiate," he explained. "I will, and we can do health care. We can do a lot of great things together."

Republicans oppose a single-payer system, and the plan would need Trump's signature to become law. The Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that it would raise federal health care subsidies from $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion by 2030, though out-of-pocket costs for patients would fall.

news.title: Trump administration slams Australian social media law as a setback for free speech
news.text:
The US has criticised Australia’s proposed sweeping online safety legislation that requires social media companies to take steps to protect users from serious harm.

The US argued that the legislation’s vaguely defined rules and penalties of up to five per cent of global revenue could force American technology companies to censor lawful speech and impose disproportionate compliance costs on them.

The legislation, negotiated between prime minister Anthony Albanese’s Labor government and the Greens, would allow individuals to sue social media platforms if breaches of their duty of care cause harm. 

It would also require platforms to let users opt out of algorithm-driven feeds, assess risks posed by addictive design features and establish a digital complaints ombudsman.

US ambassador David Brat suggested that Washington could take action over the bill, which is expected to pass the Senate. 

In a social media post, he said freedom of expression was fundamental to a free society and that “protecting it is a US priority”.

“Today I met Minister for Communications Anika Wells and laid out the Trump Administration’s well-known objections to the Digital Duty of Care Legislation. Vaguely defined ‘harms’, backed by penalties of up to five per cent of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” he said in a statement shared on X. 

“As Australia’s largest foreign investor, the US is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”

The proposed reforms also include stronger privacy protections and expanded powers for Australia’s eSafety Commissioner to remove harmful content, including AI-generated sexualised images and material promoting violence, harassment and hatred against women.

“This is seismic reform, this ‌is urgent reform and this is reform we will deliver to Australians in parliament this week,” Ms Wells told reporters earlier.

“That will make it abundantly clear that this is not about disagreeing with feminism or about expressing an opinion,” she said. “It is about protecting children from content that promotes hatred of women, violence, coercion, intimidation, harassment, death.”

Greens communications spokeswoman Sarah Hanson-Young said: “Big tech will face big consequences when they fail to keep Australians safe online. Social media giants will pay billions of dollars for the harm they cause.

“Today the parliament is drawing a line in the sand. The era of big tech profiting off the harm of Australians and getting away with it is over.”

Ms Wells had previously said that US president Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform would fall under the new laws, while stressing that the government remained committed to “constructive dialogue” with Washington. 

She reiterated that position after meeting Mr Brat on Tuesday, saying: “I think we would say there are points of differences, and we’re ironing them out.” 

Mr Albanese said in parliament: “It’s about Australia ⁠taking action on the side of parents and children, not foreign-owned tech companies.

“World-leading reform and we are getting it done. Just like we have led the world when it comes to the ⁠under-16s social media ban. This is the next step.”
news.summary: US ambassador to Australia says freedom of expression fundamental to free society
news.author: Maroosha Muzaffar

news.title: Keeping India a ‘half’: The world is G2.5, but America and China are bracing for G3
news.text:
When Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen last week, several geostrategic experts, particularly in the West, rushed to call it ‘Yalta 2.0’, aimed at dividing the world into respective “spheres of influence”.
But, then, Shenzhen was no Yalta. In 1945, three triumphant powers were attempting to carve up the world. In Shenzhen, three deeply insecure powers appeared to be scrambling to preserve and, wherever possible, extend their influence. Yalta was an assertion of power; Shenzhen was as much an expression of anxiety and self-preservation. One was about shaping the emerging world order; the other seemed all about arresting the erosion of an existing one.
The just-released Asia Power Index 2026, prepared by the Lowy Institute, has further punctured the Yalta thesis. According to the Index, India, that is Bharat, is now Asia’s third most powerful nation — a distant third, admittedly, but comfortably ahead of Japan and Russia. Any contemporary Yalta that excludes India would, therefore, be an exercise in geopolitical self-deception. More importantly, power today is far too diffused and decentralised for three men in a room to determine the destiny of the world.
India, with an overall power score of 40.5 out of 100, has emerged as Asia’s sole “major power”, while the United States and China occupy the “superpower” category, with scores of 78.9 and 73.6, respectively.
ASIA POWER INDEX: In 2026, the top five countries for overall power in Asia are the United States, China, India, Japan and Russia. Australia remains sixth in this year’s ranking.
https://t.co/qrk0mc8Z8y https://t.co/VVdHc9oo5H
— The Lowy Institute (@LowyInstitute) November 22, 2026
The Index reminded me of an article by Hindol Sengupta, ‘The G2.5 World’, published last October in The Sunday Guardian, in which he argued that America was slowly “accepting that it has to accommodate China, and in the remaining space, India is jostling in”. Sengupta took this argument forward in his recent article in Firstpost, arguing that China has not so much displaced America as joined it, and that India has emerged as the third pivot of the international system, being wooed by both Washington and Beijing but beholden to neither.
Sengupta seems to have got it right. Except that there may be a twist in the tale.
What if the two superpowers, instead of wooing the “half”, increasingly find common cause in cutting it to size? What if their mutual rivalry coexists with a shared apprehension about the emergence of a third pole? Could Washington and Beijing, adversaries in the struggle for global supremacy, become unlikely partners in resisting the dilution of their privileged status?
The Asia Power Index offers some interesting clues. It says, “India consolidated its position as a major power in 2026... The gap in power between India and China reached its narrowest point since the inception of the Asia Power Index in 2018 — though China’s power remains 80 per cent higher than India’s.”
Despite a “mixed economic year”, with its “Economic Capability” score dipping marginally to 26.4 points, India retained its third position. A weakening rupee, a structural change in the International Monetary Fund’s measurement of economies and a nearly $20 billion decline in outbound investment weighed on its performance. Still, India became more influential in Asia — and beyond. The relative stability of its regional trade and investment ties made it one of only five countries whose “Economic Relationships” score did not decline. Its “Defence Networks” score rose to 18.6 points, with greater regional defence engagement and BrahMos missile sales to Southeast Asia lifting it two places to ninth. Its “Cultural Influence” score climbed to 43.8 points, driven by improvements in cultural projection, information flows and people exchanges.
What Washington and Beijing would be watching particularly closely, and with concern, however, is New Delhi’s performance in three categories: “Future Resources”, “Military Capability” and “Defence Networks”. Together, they point to a country whose geopolitical weight is only going to increase in future. Its ‘Diplomatic Influence’, meanwhile, remained its strongest measure, holding remarkably steady at 70.3 points in a year when most countries faltered.
For the two superpowers, the real concern may not be Delhi’s present position but its future trajectory. Great powers are often more unnerved by the direction in which a rising power is moving than by the distance it has already travelled.
Even more intriguing is the Index’s “2026 Power Yield” chart, which measures the difference between a country’s actual influence and the power it would be expected to wield given its available resources. Countries such as Japan, Australia and Malaysia make efficient use of their relatively limited resources to exercise broad-based diplomatic, economic and cultural influence. India, by contrast, underperforms.
But is this necessarily a weakness? Or could it, at least in part, reflect a conscious strategic choice?
A rising power need not spend all its geopolitical capital as soon as it acquires it. India’s reluctance to get entangled in the diplomatic and military crossfires in Iran and Ukraine may be seen in this context. Despite repeated calls for a greater role, Delhi has resisted the temptation to become a protagonist in other people’s wars.
This may have cost India a few points on the power index. But nations are neither built to win annual rankings, nor is geopolitical activism necessarily synonymous with geopolitical strength. Delhi’s larger objective is to accumulate the economic, technological and military capabilities that will underpin its power for decades to come.
Here, the contrast with Pakistan is instructive. According to the Index, Islamabad ‘punched above its weight in 2026’, gaining 0.6 points to take its comprehensive power score just above 15 — the threshold for ‘middle powers’. Much of this was attributed to its shuttle diplomacy during the US-Iran ceasefire negotiations, culminating in the Islamabad Memorandum in June this year.
With this, Pakistan may have secured its moment in the diplomatic sunshine. But episodic geopolitical relevance is no substitute for structural national strength. Islamabad’s approach appears transactional and tactical; Delhi’s is geared towards the long haul.
Washington and Beijing understand this distinction. They know they must counter each other, but they also have reasons to be wary of Delhi’s rise. For the US, the prospect of a G2 world is uncomfortable; that of a G3 world is even less palatable. For China, the stakes are considerably higher. While America may eventually reconcile itself to India’s rise as a global power, given its geographical distance from Delhi, China doesn’t have this advantage: it has to contend with the emergence of a potential superpower in its immediate neighbourhood. A powerful India challenges not merely China’s global ambitions but its aspirations for Asian primacy. How can Beijing aspire to dominate the world when its pre-eminence in its own continent is increasingly contested?
The two superpowers are also acutely aware of India’s potential advantage in the three Ds — demography, democracy and diversity. China finds itself particularly vulnerable on these fronts. It faces a deepening demographic crisis and suffers from the institutional limitations of an authoritarian political system. Worse, it fares poorly on the diversity test, being an overwhelmingly Han nation with an innate distrust for outsiders.
For all its spectacular economic achievements and technological prowess, China exhibits some fundamental weaknesses. It has, for instance, failed to become a magnet for global talent. Historically, rising powers have attracted the world’s finest minds. People have sought not merely to do business with them but to build their lives and futures there. China has yet to inspire a comparable global rush.
Equally revealing is the persistent distrust of the yuan as an international currency. The currency of an aspiring superpower would ordinarily be expected to command growing global confidence, as the dollar increasingly did during America’s ascent in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Yet, China’s extraordinary economic rise has not been accompanied by a commensurate rise in global confidence in its currency. Economic might has not translated into monetary trust.
Amid all this, China’s demographic decline and economic deceleration raise an uncomfortable question: is Beijing already approaching its own version of Japan’s 1990s moment? The spectacular advances in artificial intelligence and high technology may obscure the extent of Beijing’s structural economic stress, but they do not necessarily resolve it. Technological dynamism and economic stagnation are not mutually exclusive.
At a time when America is showing signs of relative decline and China signs of plateauing, India’s rise assumes greater significance. None of this guarantees Delhi’s eventual emergence as a superpower. Demographic potential is not destiny, just as democracy and diversity do not automatically translate into national strength. But these attributes, combined with India’s growing economic and military capabilities, give the established powers sufficient reason to take that possibility seriously — and work, often in tandem, to scuttle its rise.
The Asia Power Index establishes Delhi’s emergence as a major power. What it hints at, however, may be far more consequential. They may woo Delhi when it serves their interests and seek to constrain it when its rise threatens their own. The two superpowers need not agree on who should dominate the world to agree that their exclusive club would be better off without a third member.
And therein lies the great paradox of India’s rise: The world may already be G2.5, but Washington and Beijing could increasingly behave as though it were G3, even while publicly pretending that it remains G2. India may still be only a ‘half’ in the global superpower equation, but it could increasingly encounter the resistance reserved for a full-fledged superpower. Delhi must prepare for the burdens of big-power status well before it acquires its privileges.
The journey of a rising power is rarely paved by the goodwill of established powers. India should not expect its journey to be any different either.
(The writer is the author of ‘Bharat Rising: Dharma, Democracy, Diplomacy’ and ‘Eminent Distorians: Twists and Truths in Bharat’s History’. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

The DOJ later asked an appeals court to dismiss the civil lawsuit it had filed a month earlier to block the certification, telling the appeals court the issue was “moot.”

“The United States brought this lawsuit to ensure that the State and its officers fulfill Alaska’s obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward wrote in a filing to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last week.

The incumbent Alaska senator publicly conceded his race to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola in a post on X on Tuesday, but his location data revealed he posted it from Florida.

“Serving Alaska in the United States Senate for the past 12 years has been the honor of a lifetime, and I thank all Alaskans for that opportunity,” Sullivan, 62, wrote. “As I’ve always said I would, and out of respect for the people of Alaska and our democratic process, I accept the results certified by the Division of Elections.”
