news.title: Trump Accounts receive over $1 billion in contributions from friends and families
news.text:
Washington: Friends and family members have contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts, the tax-favoured investment accounts for children, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said as the administration encouraged parents to claim accounts opened automatically for eligible children.

More than 3 million friends and relatives contributed to the milestone, according to an announcement on the government’s Trump Accounts website. The amount excludes major philanthropic gifts such as the commitment from Michael and Susan Dell.

The announcement separately put total assets deposited in the accounts at more than $9 billion, citing family contributions, philanthropy and federal seed payments.

Bessent also said President Donald Trump had contributed personally.

“This week, the President himself joined the millions of Americans who have made personal donations to individual Trump Accounts,” he said

The announcement did not disclose the amount or identify the recipients. The contribution totals are administration figures and have not been independently audited for this report.

Created under the tax and spending law Trump signed July 4, 2025, Trump Accounts are a type of individual retirement account intended to help children build savings through investment.

Eligibility for an account is broader than eligibility for the government’s initial $1,000 payment.

A child can qualify for an account with a valid Social Security number if the child will remain under 18 through the end of the year in which it is established. The federal payment is limited to US citizens born between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2028, who have valid Social Security numbers.

Parents or other authorised adults can claim an automatically opened account through the official app without submitting Form 4547. However, they must separately elect the $1,000 government contribution using that form, the Internal Revenue Service says.

Treasury announced October 1 that automatic enrollment had made accounts available to more than 60 million additional eligible children.

Parents or guardians must claim those accounts before managing them or allowing contributions from relatives, friends and employers. Eligible children must also have their accounts claimed before receiving the federal seed payment, Treasury said.

The program has also attracted large philanthropic commitments. Michael and Susan Dell announced a $6.25 billion pledge in December 2025 to provide $250 each to 25 million children age 10 and younger living in ZIP codes with median incomes below $150,000, according to the White House.

That announced commitment is separate from Tuesday’s milestone for contributions by friends and family members.

news.title: US set to announce new tariffs on major trading partners
news.text:
The United States plans to announce new tariffs on several countries on Wednesday, according to the BBC. The US new tariffs would hit many of America’s biggest trading partners.

China, the European Union and Japan are among at least 14 economies likely to be affected.

The move follows a White House probe known as the “Section 301” investigation. The administration launched it in March, after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.

Tariffs have become a key policy of Trump’s presidency. He argues that they will boost American manufacturing and create jobs.

In April 2025, shortly after his return to the White House, Trump shocked the world with sweeping tariffs on global trading partners. Although the courts later struck those tariffs down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued at the time that excess production abroad was pushing out American factories and scaring off investment.

Under the new plan, countries will face different tax rates on their goods. The rates will depend on the deals each country has already made with Trump.

The announcement is likely to raise tension between the US and China, the world’s two largest economies. The two countries are still locked in a trade dispute.

Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met last week. Even so, the two sides have not fully settled their differences, and their interim agreement is due to expire on January 10.

Before the meeting in Shenzhen, the US accused China of not fully keeping to the terms it agreed in South Korea in October 2025. Washington said Beijing had fallen short on its promises, “particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals.”

However, on Tuesday, China extended its pause on a ban on exports of critical minerals, including gallium, germanium and antimony, until January 27. Without the extension, the ban would have taken effect on Friday.

Meanwhile, critics say the Trump administration’s tariffs have pushed up prices for American shoppers and harmed the global economy.
news.summary:
The United States is preparing to announce new tariffs on several of its biggest trading partners on Wednesday. China, the European Union and Japan are among at least 14 economies expected to be affected.

news.title: Trump signals narrowing window for Iran strikes: ‘We have funding through the end of January’
news.text: U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday that funding for the war against Iran was secured through roughly the end of January, acknowledging that his military options could become more limited when Democrats take control of Congress following the Republicans’ defeat in the midterm elections. Trump also addressed the differences between Israeli and U.S. war objectives, making clear that overthrowing Iran’s clerical regime was not his goal, although he considered it achievable. Speaking in the Oval Office at the White House, Trump lashed out at congressional Democrats threatening to bring the military campaign against Iran to an end. “They’ll take a total win and make it a loss,” he said, claiming that Iran’s navy, air force, air defenses and leadership had been decimated. He argued that ending the campaign prematurely would turn what he considered a military victory into a defeat. Trump questioned how Democrats could justify such a decision politically, insisting that the United States had already won and could end the war whenever it chose. Asked whether his window for ordering further strikes without additional constraints was narrowing, Trump acknowledged that funding was available until approximately the end of January, while reiterating his opposition to a premature end to the campaign. Trump’s remarks come as Israel presses the U.S. administration to resume strikes against Iran, partly over concerns about Tehran’s developing chemical weapons capabilities. In recent days, Trump has said he is in no rush to make a decision on Iran and would reassess developments after the start of the new year. Trump launched the war against Iran in February, initially estimating that it would last about four weeks. A ceasefire took effect in April, and in June the sides signed a memorandum of understanding intended to end the conflict. The agreement collapsed several weeks later following Iranian attacks on commercial shipping. Earlier this month, Trump said the war was effectively over from a military standpoint but made clear that he intended to maintain the blockade of Iranian ports to pressure Tehran into reaching a nuclear agreement. Asked about Israel’s ambition to overthrow Iran’s clerical regime, Trump described the objective as “probably doable,” but stressed that it was not his own. “I just don’t want them to have a nuclear weapon,” he said, explaining that regime change had never been a criterion for his campaign. It was not the first time Trump had distanced himself from that objective. As recently as Saturday, he told Fox News that he had never attached much importance to who governed Iran. Trump has sent conflicting messages on the issue throughout the war: At its outset, he urged Iranians to take control of their government, but in an address to the nation in April, he clarified that regime change was not among the war’s objectives. Trump also addressed Iran’s announcement this week that it intends to seek compensation from the United States over the strike on a girls’ school in the southern Iranian city of Minab on the opening day of Operation Roaring Lion, which killed more than 150 people, most of them children, according to Iranian authorities. Trump countered that Washington should seek compensation for victims of Iranian actions over the years, claiming that the regime had killed 75,000 protesters over the past seven months. He argued that the United States had the stronger compensation claim and said the conflict dated back to 1979, presenting himself as the only U.S. president willing to take military action. Kim’s ‘love letters’ and Trump’s laughter over Zelensky’s deadline Trump also addressed tensions with North Korea, saying the exchange of letters with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un that characterized his first term in office could resume at any moment. He denied that Kim had ignored his attempts to establish contact, following a Wall Street Journal report that a letter he had sent to the North Korean leader had been returned unopened by Pyongyang’s representative at the United Nations. Trump said the correspondence could resume immediately, although the two leaders had not exchanged letters recently. He maintained that their relationship remained good. Asked whether Kim had rebuffed his outreach ahead of his visit to Asia last week, Trump denied being ignored, saying the two would eventually meet but that the timing had not been right. The U.S. president burst out laughing when asked about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s claim that U.S. negotiators wanted to secure a peace agreement between Kyiv and Moscow by January. “Who said that?” Trump asked, exchanging a glance with a senior aide in the room. He then questioned what Zelensky expected him to do. Trump made clear that he was not committed to any timetable for ending the war in Ukraine, saying he would welcome an immediate agreement but that “it takes two to tango.” He argued that the conflict did not directly affect the United States and that Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky had appeared willing to reach an agreement at different times, with one often reluctant when the other was ready.
news.summary: Trump warns Democratic control of Congress could restrict his military options as Israel pushes for renewed strikes over Iran’s chemical weapons capabilities; he says toppling the ayatollahs’ regime is possible but insists it is not a US war objective

news.title: Jensen Huang's Return To Nvidia Brings Open-Weight AI Debate To Fore In US
news.text: Nvidia's leadership crisis has thrust a tech industry squabble over open-weight AI models into the spotlight, where CEO Jensen Huang has become one of Washington's loudest voices for US development of a technology now dominated by Chinese companies.Nvidia's board announced on Monday that it would reinstate Huang as CEO, following his resignation over reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman who news reports said was suspected of spying for the Chinese government.Before the scandal erupted, Huang had pushed the US Congress and the Trump administration to support American companies developing open-weight AI models, which would align with his company's commercial interests, although a debate has raged over the models' implications for US national security.President Donald Trump's administration supports open-weight AI systems because they give startups dependable and cheaper options outside proprietary AI tools from providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic."The Trump Administration's clear and long-standing policy has been strong support for" open-weight AI models, a White House official said in a statement to Reuters on Tuesday.Trump and Vice President JD Vance personally intervened in the Nvidia board's decision to reinstate Huang in part because they viewed him as the protector of US-made open-weight AI models, people familiar with the matter said on Monday. The White House did not comment on the connection between the support for Huang and open-weight models.Open-weight AI models, unlike closed models, make core components publicly available for users to download, modify and adapt for specific tasks. Such models broaden demand for Nvidia's chips and computing infrastructure beyond a handful of leading AI model developers, providing a business opportunity for Huang's company.Executives from closed-model developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI have expressed skepticism of open-weight models, according to their public statements, creating a schism in the AI sector. Anthropic and OpenAI earn revenue by selling access to proprietary systems whose underlying technology they control."Any kind of political headwinds against Huang and Nvidia could be a harbinger for a crackdown on open weights, which is not good for little tech and companies that are trying to have a fighting chance of disrupting some of the incumbents," said Luther Lowe of Y Combinator, a Silicon Valley incubator and startup fund.In a letter earlier this year, Huang urged the US government to avoid "premature restrictions" on open-weight tools. A coalition of companies co-signed the letter, including venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, Microsoft and Palantir. Anthropic declined to sign on.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said he disagreed with parts of Huang's statement, arguing that increasingly capable open-weight models could create security risks, including helping users to exploit publicly available information to develop biological weapons. In a statement, he said that "sufficiently capable" AI tools could use publicly available materials to spread infectious diseases.US competitiveness with China is also a key aspect of the policy debate in Washington. Chinese models such as DeepSeek and Alibaba's offerings have won American business users because they are often cheaper than proprietary systems from OpenAI and Anthropic while performing comparably on many tasks.The Trump administration has taken a few steps to support the US open-weight ecosystem, including public statements from White House tech adviser Michael Kratsios. The Trump administration over the summer told leading AI model developers that it would not put open-weight AI models through voluntary government safety tests, Reuters reported, a win for proponents such as Nvidia who do not want such models to face additional regulatory hurdles.The administration is separately considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese-made AI models, including open-weight tools, Reuters reported last week.Two Republican chairs of House committees involved in AI policy urged the Trump administration last week to go further, by barring US government agencies and contractors from using Chinese open-weight AI models. They want the government to give US companies developing open-weight models more access to computing resources, arguing that expanding the open-weight ecosystem in the US is a national security imperative in the AI race against China."The time to act is now, while we still have the opportunity and leverage to do so," House Homeland Security Committee chair Andrew Garbarino and China Committee chair John Moolenaar said in a joint statement.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Pentagon hires conservative contractors to audit military base schools and pilot 'classical' PE
news.text:
The Defense Department is continuing to revamp the schools it operates for military families to meet conservative education ideals — auditing curriculum and policies in all schools and piloting a so-called “classical” physical education course at two U.S. campuses.

The Department of Defense Education Activity operates about 160 schools across 11 countries, educating roughly 70,000 students who are children of active-duty military or civilian service members. Under the leadership of Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has sought to use the schools as models for the broader Republican education agenda. Those goals include restrictions on instruction about race and gender, along with an emphasis on patriotic values and classical learning. 

Now, the agency has begun issuing contracts to companies well-connected to conservative ideals, with no outside competition.

In October, the department approved a contract for a curriculum audit, saying it was complying with an executive order from President Donald Trump aimed at limiting how schools teach about race and gender. It awarded the $5.7 million contract to American Education Solutions, without seeking other bids. The firm was founded by Jordan Adams, whose past work involved consulting with conservative-led school boards in Pennsylvania and Texas to overhaul curriculum. 

Separately, the department awarded a contract for just over $100,000 to Iliad Athletics to pilot a classical physical education program. Classical education broadly focuses on critical thinking, citizenship and, often, writers from ancient Greece, Rome and other Western civilizations. Inspired by traditional Greek athletics, the P.E. course will include running, jumping, climbing, carrying and throwing, Iliad Athletics said. 

A spokesperson for the Department of Defense Education Activity said the agency regularly reviews its academic programs and makes improvements. The audit will review "curriculum, instruction, and professional learning, helping ensure these areas remain rigorous, effective, and aligned with the needs of students and educators,” the department said in a statement. 

But two employees of the Pentagon's education division, speaking anonymously for fear of retribution, said a system-wide review by a consultant is without precedent. Typically, schools work with a national accreditor to evaluate and develop standards for subjects.

 Contractor says it audits schools to ‘Do No Harm’ 

On its website, American Education Solutions advertises a curriculum adoption, analysis and development service. It criticizes curricula used in American schools, saying they are “content-light, employ pedagogical practices not supported by the science of learning, and eschew the patriotic civic role of public education.” 

The company also offers an audit to ensure schools “Do No Harm." 

“The intellectual and character formation of children is a serious responsibility for school systems,” the website says. “As with medicine, the first requirement is to do no harm — both pedagogically and with respect to parents as first educators. AES reviews school systems to ensure this is the case.” 

In a statement, the Pentagon lauded the approach, saying it “preserves effective practices while identifying opportunities for thoughtful improvement."

AES did not respond to questions and said the company does not “share work for past, current or pending clients without authorization.” 

 PE course to focus on fitness, rather than sports 

The new classical P.E. course will be offered at LeJeune High School in North Carolina and Quantico Middle High School in Virginia. In a statement announcing the partnership with the military, Iliad Athletics described the course as focused on functional physical fitness rather than introducing students to sports. 

In addition to physical activity, the course includes a “character development program," which highlights a weekly virtue and gives examples of historical figures who lived it out. 

As with the auditing contract, Iliad's hire did not involve competitive bids. Instead, the Pentagon said the company was the only one that could meet its requirements at the time.

Patrick Whalen, CEO of Iliad Athletics, said in an email he was not aware of any other programs like the one the company offers. 

In a statement, a Pentagon official said no company receives preferential treatment.

“The War Department always looks for solutions to benefit the warfighter, not any pre-selected entity,” the statement said. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”

 Hegseth promotes classical education 

Hegseth has a longtime interest in classical education, especially in a version of the teaching style that incorporates Christian history and virtues. As defense secretary, he has pushed to advance those views. 

U.S. military academies now accept the Classic Learning Test, a college entrance exam that positions itself as a classical alternative to the SAT. In September, defense schools announced they would give 100 vouchers to students to take the CLT. This month, the agency announced the test would be widely available to students as a college readiness assessment. 

This summer, schools operated by the department announced they would begin offering a new online course on Western Civilization, using a text that some scholars said presents a misleading portrait of historical events. In particular, the book often portrays Western civilization and Christianity as one and the same, and it selectively highlights details to frame Islam as a violent threat to both.

The course's textbook includes suggested lesson plans developed in partnership with Hillsdale College, a conservative Christian school in Michigan that has also developed influential materials for K-12 schools.

The new Pentagon contractors have ties to Hillsdale, too. 

Adams, the consultant, graduated from Hillsdale and worked in K-12 curriculum development for the college, including on the Trump-aligned 1776 Project, a free curriculum for schools that was created in response to what the college described as “the weaponization of history.” The content has been criticized for downplaying slavery and for describing the Jamestown colony as a failed communist project. 

Whalen, the Iliad Athletics CEO, previously worked in the college president’s office. 

Along with the curriculum changes, leadership at the military's education system has also been overhauled. The schools are now led by Matthew Kirby, who was promoted from his former position as the system's Americas regional director. Kirby is the founder and former CEO of Liberty Classical Schools, an Atlanta-based network of charter schools.

Early in Trump's second administration, Defense schools also removed books from libraries that covered topics like race, gender and democracy. The ACLU filed a lawsuit and was partially successful in overturning the book bans at a handful of schools.

news.summary: The Defense Department continues to revamp its schools for military families to align with conservative education ideals

news.title: Trump Praises El-Sayed After Medicare for All Twist: 'He's a Smart Guy'
news.text: President Donald Trump praised Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed as the Democrat continues to push for Medicare for All, even floating “TrumpCare” as a potential name for the plan. “He’s a smart guy,” Trump said about El-Sayed while chuckling in an exclusive interview with the New York Post on Tuesday. “He did a good job. He actually did a very good job.” “I know I’ll be meeting with him,” Trump also told the outlet. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.” Earlier this month, the Michigan Democrat posted images of the mock TrumpCare card on X, saying, "This is a message for @realDonaldTrump. Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave." El-Sayed, a physician, campaigned heavily on the Medicare for All platform, saying it should be automatic for everyone and accepted everywhere. Before his senatorial campaign, El-Sayed ran Detroit's health department. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed's transition team via email late Tuesday night for comment. What To Know As the final two years of Trump's second term come into focus, he told reporters last week that there is a "real possibility" to get things done with Democrats, specifically pointing to healthcare. In his interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, he recited a similar tune, adding, “I’m just going to veto everything there is, and then at some point I think they’re going to want to negotiate. I will, and we can do health care. We can do a lot of great things together.” He later told the outlet, “Obamacare hasn’t worked, and I’d love to get great health care for the people of our country.” Robert Y. Shapiro, professor of political science at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs, told Newsweek on Tuesday, "We should not put it past Trump to want to do something big on health care that he can claim credit for as his long awaited replacement for his much despised Obamacare." In an interview with NPR earlier this month, El-Sayed said he had not spoken with Trump at that point yet. "Donald, if you're listening, there's a lot we could work on," he said. "Happy to have a meeting. Let's figure out what we can work on and get done." El-Sayed also touched on naming healthcare legislation after the president in the interview with the outlet, adding, "Put his name on it. He'll probably pass it. I'm not above doing that. I don't care what it's called." During the midterm elections run-up, Trump campaigned on behalf of numerous Republicans including El-Sayed's opponent Mike Rogers. The president repeatedly took swipes at El-Sayed, even calling him a "radical jihadist." Republicans faced crushing losses during the midterms, which resulted in the party losing its majority in both the U.S. House and Senate. Even as Democrats control both chambers next year, an effort to get a single-payer healthcare plan to Trump's desk faces an uphill fight. The party’s left-leaning flank, including Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, seems to comprise the sole backers of the idea, and Democratic leaders have not overwhelmingly committed to passing it. Since being elected to his first term in office, Trump has swayed a bit on single-payer healthcare. In 2018, he called the proposal "Medicare for None." In November 2025, Trump ripped into insurance companies, saying he would not sign anything that sent them money. In a post to X on Monday, El-Sayed reaffirmed his goal for getting the idea across the finish line. "The point of winning elections is to do something good with the seat. The point for me is to pass Medicare for All. I really don't care who puts their name on it if that's what it takes," he said. According to the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker, the average health consumption expenditures in the United States per person in 2024 was $14,775. This far exceeds Switzerland, which was second to the U.S., with $9,963 per person. The comparable country average is $7,860, the tracker shows. news.summary: Trump said that he knows he'll meet with El-Sayed and maybe there is a compromise in the middle the two can land on.

news.title: Trump Says Toppling Iran’s Regime Is ‘Probably Doable’ but Not His Goal
news.text:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Israel’s goal of toppling Iran’s Islamic regime is “probably doable,” but he stressed that regime change has never been his objective, reiterating that his priority is preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

In an exclusive Oval Office interview with the New York Post, Trump also revealed that his military campaign against Iran is funded through January, warning that congressional Democrats could turn an American victory into a defeat by moving to curtail operations.

“I just don’t want them to have a nuclear weapon. I was never for or against regime change, that was never a criteria for me,” he told the outlet.

Trump’s remarks come after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu directed the Israeli military, the Mossad intelligence agency, and the broader defense establishment last month to pursue the overthrow of the Iranian regime.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz briefed reporters Tuesday on preparations for potential renewed military action against Iran, with Israeli media reporting that the Mossad is spearheading efforts to bring about regime change.

Meanwhile, NBC News reported Tuesday that Trump administration officials are debating whether targeting senior Iranian leaders could help bring the conflict to an end, with some arguing that such action could increase pressure on Tehran and others warning that it could undermine negotiations.

Trump has yet to make a final decision on the matter, according to the report.

Speaking during Tuesday’s White House turkey pardon ceremony, the president underscored the extent of Iran’s military losses and the effectiveness of the ongoing U.S. naval blockade.

“They have no army. They have no navy. They have no air force. They’ve been pretty well wiped out,” Trump said, adding that Iran retains “a little capacity to fire missiles.”

The president hailed the operation as the “greatest naval blockade in history,” saying no Iranian ship had gotten through since its establishment, apart from a temporary moratorium.

Earlier this month, Trump described the conflict as “effectively over” militarily while maintaining economic pressure on Tehran.

The administration has since intensified its efforts to financially cripple the Islamic Republic, unveiling sweeping sanctions Monday targeting the regime’s shadow banking network.

“Iran’s economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared, describing Iran’s shadow banking system as “the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime.”

Trump nevertheless signaled last week that further major military action could come after the new year.

Addressing the prospect of congressional Democrats restricting his military options once they assume power in January, Trump warned the Post that doing so would squander the gains already achieved against Iran.

“They’ll take a total win and make it a loss,” he said.

“I don’t know how they could do that politically, because we have a win. We can put that war to bed anytime we want.”

Vice President JD Vance similarly emphasized last week that the administration’s objective is to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, vowing that Trump would not allow the conflict to become another “forever war.”

President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Israel’s goal of toppling Iran’s Islamic regime is “probably doable,” but stressed that regime change has never been his objective, reiterating that his priority is preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

news.title: Elon Musk Discovers That 'American Elections Are Not Just About Money'
news.text:
Elon Musk, the world's richest man, spent nearly half a billion dollars in a vain attempt to help Republicans win this month's midterm elections. "I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it," he told The New York Times last week.

Contrary to what advocates of stricter campaign finance regulation often imply, Musk noted that "American elections are not just about money." That point was repeatedly confirmed by midterm races that Republicans lost, sometimes by a lot, despite large spending advantages.

"Republicans have an enormous financial edge in this year's midterms," Times reporter Shane Goldmacher noted in October. In the seven U.S. Senate races that the Cook Political Report described as toss-ups, Goldmacher reported, "Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising by $947 million to $625 million"—"a breathtaking advantage of more than $320 million in the key races that could determine which party wins control of the Senate."

Democrats won all those Senate races, plus 15 more. In Texas, for example, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton by 12 points, even though pro-Paxton spending, including $212 million that Musk contributed, exceeded pro-Talarico spending by about 35 percent.

Money clearly was not enough to make up for the manifest defects of a scandal-plagued candidate like Paxton, who also suffered from his close association with President Donald Trump. By contrast, that association enabled Paxton to prevail against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary.

In a contest dominated by the MAGA faithful, Trump's favor easily overcame Cornyn's vastly superior financial resources. Although Cornyn and his supporters outspent Paxton and his allies by more than 3 to 1, Paxton trounced Cornyn in their head-to-head match, winning by more than 27 points.

In addition to beating Paxton in the general election, Democrats won every other statewide contest in Texas, including the elections for governor, lieutenant governor, and attorney general. That sweep was remarkable enough given recent Texas political history, and it was especially striking because Republicans outspent Democrats by more than 5 to 1 overall and by nearly 8 to 1 in the gubernatorial race, where Gina Hinojosa beat the incumbent, Greg Abbott, by seven points.

Beyond Texas, big spending likewise was no guarantee of victory. In the Ohio gubernatorial race, Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy and his supporters outspent Democratic nominee Amy Acton and her allies by nearly 3 to 1. Acton won by eight points.

Republican candidate Rick Jackson spent more than $200 million of his own money on his campaign for governor of Georgia. As of October 20, spending on Jackson's behalf totaled about $235 million, compared to $30 million for Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms. Despite that 8-to-1 financial advantage, Jackson lost the race by more than eight points.

Notwithstanding such conspicuous counterexamples, a 2024 study of House elections from 2000 to 2018 found that campaign spending was positively associated with victory. But as in earlier research, the association was stronger for challengers than for incumbents.

In general, a 1 percent increase in campaign spending corresponded with a 6.5-point increase in the probability of winning. But for incumbents, the "marginal effect" was negative, especially when it came to contributions by special-interest groups.

The authors echoed the explanation offered by other researchers: Although incumbents start with big advantages, including the name recognition, publicity, support networks, and pork associated with their offices, they face "diminishing returns for the money spent on campaigning," such that "higher campaign spending does not help incumbents much to secure a seat." Challengers, by contrast, see "increasing marginal returns for each dollar spent" as they strive to overcome the benefits of incumbency.

Given that difference, limits on campaign spending are unlikely to reduce the dauntingly high reelection rates for members of Congress, which averaged about 93 percent for the House and 88 percent for the Senate from 2010 through 2024. To the contrary, such restrictions would further undermine competitiveness by making it even harder to throw the bums out.

news.title: Meet George Jensen
news.text:
Every human being is precious; God made them all. But we have seen throughout history that some people seem to be so unique in their skills and abilities that others simply can’t replace them. The Allies intentionally placed General George Patton across from the Pas-de-Calais because they did not plan to attack there. The Germans reasoned that the Allies would never start an epic battle to retake Europe without their best general, so they fell for the feint, and Patton joined the battle in France a month after the successful Normandy landings.

I don’t pretend to have some proprietary knowledge on the downfall/rise of Jensen Huang, formerly and presently of NVIDIA. There appeared to be three levels of perfidy involved:

1. Personal: Based on reports, Huang was involved with various women whose last names were not Mrs. Huang, though the Chinese lady was close.

2. Corporate: One or more of his dalliances may have involved coworkers, and this is usually a third rail in most companies. Also, stories have circulated that Huang did not win the Ms. Congeniality Award and could be a jerk toward coworkers.

3. National Security: Scott Bessent may have been the most outspoken in suggesting that Huang and NVIDIA might have sidestepped U.S. trade sanctions and sent China advanced chips that it should not have received. The issue of one of the women being a “Chinese spy” has raised the specter of China benefiting from the relationship. Donald Trump told the NVIDIA board that there was little likelihood that Huang would be prosecuted.

So why did Huang quit the company that he made into the most critical in the all-important AI space? Because he was frequently seen and photographed with a Chinese asset? Because of moral turpitude? Because of embarrassment? Whatever the reason, he is now back. Apple almost died without Steve Jobs. When he left and then came back, he found a company in disarray, one that was a few months away from running out of money. He once again became CEO and made Apple into the electronics juggernaut we know today. So will NVIDIA continue on as before? Will there be some lingering distrust? I have never before seen a company or the NASDAQ take off like a SpaceX rocket.

When my friend and I had our first startup, our investors insisted on “key-man insurance.” If anything happened to one of us, their investment was covered. And there are truly individuals who seem somewhat irreplaceable in their companies or surroundings. Elon Musk is Tesla, and he is SpaceX. Obviously, he has highly competent engineers and executives working for him, but in the end, it is his vision, his drive, and his efforts and money that push all of his companies forward to flying cars and catchable rockets. A setback for him is a recipe for future success. Most others would have quit the rocket game after a few explosions. Musk didn’t, and now he has put up more mass of satellites into space than all other companies and countries combined since the beginning of space exploration.

So how will Huang’s reintegration work out? Does he have to do some pathetic apology tour? Does he have to show five minutes of official contrition? Probably not. The NVIDIA board apparently had to swallow its pride: he was the one guy who made everything work, and like Tom Brady going to Tampa Bay, the success might have gone wherever Huang could have ended up if they did not UNANIMOUSLY return him to his various positions in the company. “You’re a lout and a cheat. Welcome home!”

What would have happened if Huang had joined Elon Musk at Terrafab? What if he had taken all of his knowledge, connections, and insights in order to build NVIDIA II— the revenge company? NVIDIA is one of the few companies today that the U.S. government might deem a national security asset. If Billy Bob’s Tex-Mex restaurant or Joey’s Gas and Lube Emporium goes under, the Republic will probably soldier on. If China becomes the dominant force in AI chips (something that still seems far off right now…), then the U.S. might be looking at the losing end of a global balance of power. Donald Trump used the force of his personality and the gravity of his office to get NVIDIA to take back its wayward CEO. He knows that AI/SI leadership is critical for American dominance in economic and military matters. The U.S. government moved from spectator to participant in a very high-stakes game. NVIDIA also had to know that Huang was not going to retire and learn knitting. Better to keep the company’s “enemy” close rather than let him take others to set up shop elsewhere.

The U.S. was, in some ways, in a pickle. On the one hand, NVIDIA is a private company and should be shielded from excessive governmental interference. On the other hand, NVIDIA is the key to America remaining the leader in AI, the most important technology of the present and near future. The U.S. held its nose and brought in Nazis to build rockets down in Alabama. It did the same to get spies into the Soviet Union. Was it the right thing to do? Morally, one would have a strong argument against the policy; by geopolitics at the dawn of the Cold War and the Space Race, it would seem to have been the smart move. I did not expect Donald Trump to directly intervene with the board as he did. I didn’t expect him or anyone around him to make that phone call to get the former CEO back into his comfy office. But the U.S. needs AI chip leadership. That leadership does not necessarily have to come from NVIDIA, though they are the current reigning champ. Even if Huang had teamed up with Elon Musk, it would have taken time to get their lines up and running. Right now, time is everything, and waiting a year until Terrafab is making NVIDIA-level chips is too much. So Donald Trump made the call, the board reversed itself, and Huang can drop his request for unemployment payments.

The whiplash of the markets is a strange thing. I once spoke to a banker, and he said that institutional investors can sway markets for their own financial considerations. The old “P/E ratio” model means nothing when looking at Anthropic: its present income trajectory is a pittance in comparison to its $1.5 trillion valuation. These market gyrations are insane. The loss of $2.3 trillion in NVIDIA value with Huang’s exit, followed by its rise by $1 trillion after the announcement of his return, is new territory, never recorded in the annals of public markets.

So what really caused Huang to lose his job? The women? The possible espionage? The workplace bullying? And also why now? He was with that supposed spy for quite some time, with many public pictures of the pair. Can NVIDIA recover all of its market value in just a few days or weeks? Can it innovate and continue to lead the all-critical AI chip race for U.S. dominance? Will Huang’s return justify the massive return to value of NVIDIA shares?

news.title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan seeks execution delay, says he was defending Taliban
news.text: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution, saying he intends to argue that he was defending the Taliban from an unlawful US military attack.In a court filing signed by Hasan on Tuesday, he said he intended to demonstrate that the military court’s judgment and his death sentence had been obtained and were being maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights.The filing could delay the Trump administration’s plans to execute Hasan on December 3. A hearing has been scheduled for Wednesday morning.Hasan, who is representing himself with assistance from lawyers at the American Civil Liberties Union’s Capital Punishment Project, said he intended to continue representing himself in the legal fight.Hasan wants to revive defence barred at trialOne of Hasan’s central arguments is that he was prevented from presenting a defence that his actions were legally justified because he was trying to protect the Afghan Taliban from what he described as an unlawful attack by the US Army.Hasan had argued that he was acting in “defense of others”, according to court documents. However, the military judge barred him from presenting that argument during his 2013 trial.After dismissing his lawyers and choosing to represent himself, Hasan largely remained silent during the three-week trial. While the military called nearly 90 witnesses, Hasan called none in his defence and made no closing argument.A military jury found him guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder for the shooting, which left 13 people dead and 32 wounded.The case has been assigned to US district judge Tony Mattivi in Kansas, where Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth. Mattivi was nominated by president Donald Trump and confirmed by the Senate in June.What happened in the Fort Hood attack?On November 5, 2009, Hasan walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at Fort Hood, Texas, where soldiers were waiting for medical tests and preparing for deployment.He opened fire with a handgun fitted with laser sights, killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others.Hasan was shot by law enforcement officers during the attack, leaving him paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair.He was convicted by a military jury in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. The jury sentenced him to death.Execution controversy and survivors’ objectionsTrump authorised Hasan’s execution on the recommendation of defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The execution, scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the first US military execution by firing squad since World War II and the first military execution since 1961.The plan drew controversy after Hegseth announced that the execution would be public and the Pentagon confirmed it would be livestreamed. Critics from both parties raised concerns that broadcasting the execution could fuel radicalisation and turn it into a spectacle.Trump later said the execution would not be livestreamed, but that immediate family members of the victims could witness it in person if they chose.The latest court filing comes amid further dispute over who will be allowed to attend. Military officials have denied requests from three survivors of the 2009 shooting to witness the execution, citing regulations, security and space constraints.The survivors argued that the military should recognise them as victims under a broader definition that includes direct physical, emotional or financial harm. The Army rejected their appeal, saying regulations specify who may attend a military execution.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

news.title: AI Gives Hackers A Dangerous Edge, Cisco CEO Sounds Alarm Over Growing Cybersecurity Threats
news.text: Mumbai: Artificial intelligence is accelerating cybersecurity threats by enabling hackers to identify technological vulnerabilities faster than businesses can address them, Cisco Chairman and CEO Chuck Robbins has warned.The technology executive urged corporate leaders to strengthen their cybersecurity infrastructure immediately as AI-driven attacks pose growing risks to businesses and essential public services.AI Could Add $79 Billion To India's GDP In 10 Years As 89% Of Young Indians Show Interest In Using Artificial IntelligenceGrowing Cyber ThreatsIn a post on X, Robbins highlighted how artificial intelligence is transforming the cybersecurity landscape, allowing attackers to exploit weaknesses at unprecedented speed. He emphasised that organisations must prioritise security measures irrespective of their technology platforms or service providers.The warning follows recommendations from the Alliance for Critical Infrastructure (ACI), which highlighted mounting security risks arising from outdated technology, delayed software upgrades and unresolved vulnerabilities.30-Day Security ReviewThe alliance urged chief executives to assess their organisations' cybersecurity preparedness within 30 days. Businesses have been advised to identify vulnerable essential services, evaluate their ability to deploy security patches, test disaster recovery mechanisms and establish accountability for unresolved risks. The proposed deadline aims to initiate corrective measures rather than complete comprehensive cybersecurity upgrades within a month.Donald Trump Announces Plan To Ban 'Artificial Intelligence' Term In Federal Documents, Replace It With 'Super Intelligence'Critical Infrastructure At RiskIncreasing digital connectivity across electricity networks, telecommunications, data centres and water supply systems has heightened the potential impact of cyberattacks.A security breach in one sector could trigger widespread operational disruptions across interconnected industries, potentially compromising public safety and economic activity. The alliance recommended replacing unsupported technology, accelerating security updates and deploying temporary protective measures until permanent solutions become available.AI Agents Under ScrutinyThe ACI also called for tighter governance of autonomous AI agents capable of accessing corporate networks and performing tasks with limited human supervision. Companies should restrict access permissions, continuously monitor AI activities and maintain mechanisms to immediately suspend automated operations when necessary.Robbins, who serves on the alliance's board, endorsed its recommendations, underscoring the urgency of strengthening digital resilience as artificial intelligence reshapes the global cybersecurity landscape. The alliance represents several critical sectors, including energy, transportation, financial services, communications and information technology.Level up your brain the fun way. news.title: CNN Star Drops Uncensored Verdict on Scott Jennings
news.text:
Swisher, 63, was responding to a clip of Jennings on Monday’s NewsNight, where he told guest host Elie Honig, 51, to “lighten up a little and chuckle” about an AI-generated meme posted on Truth Social by President Donald Trump, 80, of Jensen Huang with blood spattered on his face, triumphantly hoisting a red bra, after Nvidia reinstated him as CEO. The image was a play on the photo captured during Trump’s attempted assassination in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024.

“Now that I am out [of] my CNN gig, I can more flatly say what I do not miss the always knuckleheaded but persistently willful compromises of Scott Jennings, who never had a boneheaded take he did not express with the smugness of Tracy Flick,” Swisher wrote on Threads, in a post that racked up nearly 16,000 likes. 

“Haha a bra is the level of discourse for maladjusted teens, not a grown-a-- man.” she closed.

Tracy Flick is the doggedly ambitious student-council hopeful played by Reese Witherspoon in the 1999 satire Election.

The meme that set her off was a parody of one of the most famous photos of Trump’s political career: the bloodied then-candidate raising his fist towards the sky mere moments after he was shot in the right ear during an assassination attempt at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. In the AI-generated spoof, it’s a defiant Huang who punches the air as Secret Service agents swarm him, red bra in hand.

Trump’s post celebrated Huang’s victorious comeback after the Nvidia co-founder stepped down on Nov. 12, when his affairs came to light. This has included one with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore’s Megaspeed, who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s board voted to reinstate him on Monday, with Trump, who owns $62 million of Nvidia stock, claiming he’d “convinced” the company to do it. 

On NewsNight on Monday, Honig had asked Jennings to explain the underwear.

“What the hell is up with the red bra? What does that mean? Interpret for us,” Honig asked Jennings. 

“Do you really need me to spell it out for you?” Jennings replied. “I mean, you could just lighten up a little and chuckle.”

“It’s a meme,” he added.

Honig then raised Corey Comperatore, the 50-year-old rally-goer killed in Butler, and asked whether Jennings thought his family would find the joke funny.

Jennings said he thought Comperatore’s family was “very grateful for how the president has interacted with him.” “The president was shot,” he said. “Does he not have the right to make light of his own situation?”

On the same broadcast, Jennings also waved off national security concerns about Huang’s return. “In this moment, my view is, I’m team America,” he said.

Jennings and CNN did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast’s request for comment. 

Swisher hasn’t hidden her growing contempt for where the network is going. In September, she said she wanted out of CNN as soon as Warner Bros. Discovery’s merger with David Ellison’s Paramount had cleared its last legal hurdle.

“F--k these guys. I don’t want to work for them. I just don’t,” she said on her Pivot podcast at the time, adding: “They don’t want me. I don’t want them, and I have been very explicit. I think they are terrible media owners. I’d rather work for Rupert Murdoch.”

In September, Swisher said she’d asked her agent to get her out of her CNN contract, which was due to run until Dec. 31, even though the network had been trying to keep her.

“They’ve been trying to keep me,” she said. “Very nicely, been trying to keep me, and I have a lot of regard for the executives there now.”

She added, “I have other things that make more money, that matter more, that have a bigger audience.”

Swisher got her wish. CNN has since released her early, according to a November Status report.
news.summary:
CNNKara Swisher has taken a swipe at a CNN colleague. 

On Tuesday, the veteran tech journalist took aim at CNN’s in-house Trump loyalist, Scott Jennings, 49, in a scathing post on Threads. 

Swisher, 63, was responding to a clip of Jennings on Monday’s NewsNight, where he told guest host Elie Honig, 51, to “lighten up a little and chuckle” about an AI-generated meme posted on Truth Social by President Donald Trump, 80, of Jensen Huang with blood spattered on his face, triumphantly hoisting a red bra, after Nvidia reinstated him as CEO. The image was a play on the photo captured during Trump’s attempted assassination in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024.

news.title: Tech outages are piling up, and AI is raising the stakes. Could this be the new normal?
news.text: Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. A communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions. And a cyberattack that breached an unclassified system at the CIA.In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal.This month alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government's Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was "zero" indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals.The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches.Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages."To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it's made them realize how many parts of their lives they've handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don't fully understand," Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. "I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way."What's gone offline recentlyOutages and technology errors have piled up across sectors.On Nov. 11, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a "latent defect" in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer.For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Nov. 13. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage - forcing it to delay departing flights the following Monday.Online banking troubles also piled up on Nov. 16. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems - causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved.The next day, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. And Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app.Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Nov. 17 "during scheduled routine maintenance."The government - as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott - have maintained there's no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack.However, an unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack, according to a person familiar with the incident who spoke to The Associated Press on Tuesday on condition of anonymity. The breach did not involve any classified information and the issue has been resolved, said the person, who was not authorized to speak by name.The breach affected a system that handles open-source intelligence, which involves the collection and analysis of publicly available data from sources including the internet, commercial satellites and private data brokers. Though the information is generally public or semi-public, open-source information can give intelligence analysts significant insight on its own or in combination with intelligence obtained from classified spying programs.It was not clear what specific information was compromised or who was responsible.The breach was first reported by The New York Times on Tuesday.AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risksMicrosoft noted that its outage did not stem from "AI / agents." It didn't specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. A press contact for Microsoft didn't immediately have further information to share when reached by The Associated Press last week. The other companies also did not provide additional comments about their disruptions when contacted by the via email last week.AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions - both heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps.For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world - leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays.President Donald Trump's director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA's outage. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month's PHP alert caused some systems to "not come back up" as expected. "That is what has happened at the NSA today," he said.Meanwhile, also last week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world's most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory Nov. 17 urging organizations to install it.At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions."As AI adoption accelerates, we are likely to witness more incidents of this nature," Raj Rajarajan, director of the Institute for Cyber Security at City St George's, University of London, said last week.He noted a lot of today's digital infrastructure wasn't originally designed to handle the "computational demands of large-scale AI services."While recent outages haven't been tied to hackers or a coordinated attack, he and others also pointed to cybersecurity risks more broadly."AI is absolutely making it way easier for attackers to go and launch cyber attacks. It is not quite as good at creating patches for bugs, like fixing problems, as it is exploiting them," said Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University's Tandon School of Engineering.In a cybersecurity report last week, Google said hackers and cyber criminals are "moving beyond basic prompting" and using increasingly sophisticated AI techniques to devise and carry out their attacks. The report, which focused on nefarious activity rather than outages, said techniques include using large language models and "agentic frameworks" to reverse engineering security patches to uncover vulnerabilities and exploit them.Unraveling one (of just a few) major players in our online livesRegardless, the latest outages offer yet more examples of the cascading effects that can erupt when a central player in tech, banking, travel or even the government runs into system errors that upend services.Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, co-chair of the U.S. Senate's Cybersecurity Caucus, acknowledged the widespread concern - and again stressed what this means in the AI era."These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences," Warner said last week. He also argued that the Trump administration hadn't shown enough interest in confronting these challenges.Still, "based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer," Warner added.
news.summary: This month alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government's Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency.

news.title: Trump Accounts hit major milestone as family contributions surpass $1 billion
news.text: Contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts have surpassed $1 billion, marking a major milestone for the children's investment program as Americans prepare for the holiday season. More than 3 million friends and family members have contributed to individual Trump Accounts — investment accounts established for children under 18 — surpassing $1 billion in personal contributions, according to a Treasury Department statement provided to FOX Business. Combined with philanthropic gifts and the federal government's $1,000 seed contributions for eligible children, total assets deposited in Trump Accounts have now surpassed $9 billion. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent praised the milestone Tuesday, saying Americans were increasingly taking advantage of the program to invest in children's financial futures. HOUSE DEM TARGETS 4 COMPANIES IN PROBE INTO TRUMP JR-LINKED 1789 CAPITAL "The American people are investing in Trump Accounts with a generosity that represents the finest instincts of our national character," Bessent said in a statement. "President Trump wanted to make it especially easy to contribute to Trump Accounts, and friends and families across the country are seizing that opportunity to help the next generation build wealth from day one," he continued. Bessent added that each contribution helps bring the promise of long-term financial security within reach of American children. He also said that President Donald Trump had joined millions of Americans making personal contributions to individual accounts. "This week, the President himself joined the millions of Americans who have made personal donations to individual Trump Accounts," Bessent said. BANK OF AMERICA CEO HONORED AT $32M FUNDRAISING EVENT AGAINST ANTISEMITISM Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers. Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a one-time $1,000 seed contribution from the federal government. While Trump Accounts have been created for eligible children under 18, parents and guardians must claim the accounts before they can manage them or enable contributions. With the holiday season approaching, friends and relatives can contribute directly to a child's Trump Account once it has been claimed. According to Treasury, contributors can use a QR code generated through the child's Trump Accounts app to make deposits. TOP TRUMP CRYPTO MEME COIN HOLDERS AWARDED WITH EXCLUSIVE DINNER EVENT Family members and friends can contribute up to a combined $5,000 per year to each account, while employers can contribute up to $2,500 annually, subject to the overall $5,000 limit. The latest milestone follows the Treasury Department's announcement last month that approximately 70 million Trump Accounts had been established for eligible children. Major philanthropic donors have also pledged support to the program, including Michael and Susan Dell, who pledged approximately $6.25 billion to provide $250 to 25 million eligible children. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Parents and guardians can claim their children's accounts through the official Trump Accounts app. Additional information is available at TrumpAccounts.gov. FOX Business' Eric Revell contributed to this report.
news.summary: Trump Accounts top $1 billion in family contributions as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Americans are investing in children's financial futures.
